items.q: Which is the odd one out among conditions the chapter associates with fish-mouth vertebrae?
items.exp: The page names osteoporosis, osteomalacia and hyperparathyroidism for fish-mouth vertebrae. Osteopetrosis is more characteristically associated with dense bone and sandwich/bone-within-bone appearances. (Book p897)

items.q: Match the following supportive entries — 1) Vitamin D3 2) Calcium 3) Lifestyle … A) 800 IU/day B) Smoking cessation/increased activity C) 1200 mg/day
items.exp: These are the source's supportive-care targets, alongside smoking cessation and more physical activity; individual intake requirements may differ. (Book p897)

items.q: Match the following drug mechanisms — 1) Bisphosphonates 2) Denosumab 3) Teriparatide … A) PTH-pathway bone formation B) RANKL inhibition C) Antiresorptive bone action
items.exp: Bisphosphonates and denosumab are antiresorptive; intermittent teriparatide promotes bone formation through the PTH receptor pathway. (Book p897)

items.q: The source ranks oral ___ ahead of ___ among bisphosphonates.
items.exp: The oral-preferred branch prints alendronate > risedronate; suitability still depends on patient characteristics. (Book p897)

items.q: A patient starts oral alendronate and asks how to reduce esophageal injury. Which instruction fits?
opts: Take fasting before breakfast and remain upright for at least 30 minutes
Take after a large meal and lie flat for 30 minutes
Take at bedtime with minimal water and immediately recline
Crush into calcium-fortified milk immediately after dinner
items.exp: The source highlights esophagitis and advises an empty stomach 30 minutes before the first meal plus 30 minutes upright; use water and follow the product instructions. (Book p897)

items.q: The IV zoledronate schedule printed for osteoporosis is ___.
items.exp: The osteoporosis branch gives 5 mg IV yearly, distinct from other indications and dosing schedules. (Book p897)

items.q: Which pair correctly distinguishes the usual oral and intravenous ibandronate osteoporosis regimens?
opts: 150 mg oral monthly; 3 mg IV every 3 months
150 mg IV monthly; 3 mg oral every 3 months
150 mg oral weekly; 3 mg IV every month
3 mg oral monthly; 150 mg IV every 3 months
items.exp: The route is erroneous: 150 mg monthly is oral; the usual IV osteoporosis regimen is 3 mg every three months. Do not use the printed IV dose clinically. (Book p897)

items.q: Match the following bisphosphonate adverse-effect clues — 1) Exposed necrotic jaw bone 2) Collapsing glomerular lesion 3) Falling serum calcium … A) Hypocalcemia B) Collapsing FSGS C) Jaw osteonecrosis
items.exp: The page lists jaw osteonecrosis, collapsing FSGS and hypocalcemia; nephrotoxicity is particularly relevant to certain IV exposures rather than an equal risk for every agent. (Book p897)

items.q: A patient with estimated GFR 24 mL/min is being considered for a bisphosphonate. What concern follows the chapter's renal warning?
opts: The value is below the source's <30 mL/min contraindication threshold
Renal function cannot affect bisphosphonate selection
The value proves an anabolic drug is also always prohibited
A larger IV dose corrects reduced renal clearance
items.exp: The source warns at GFR <30 mL/min; actual labeling varies by drug, with some using a 35 mL/min cutoff. (Book p897)

items.q: The two subcutaneous bone-forming agents named are ___ and ___.
items.exp: Teriparatide and abaloparatide activate the PTH receptor pathway; abaloparatide is a PTHrP analog, despite the source's shared recombinant-PTH heading. (Book p897)

items.q: Assess the source's treatment hierarchy: I It labels bisphosphonates first choice, teriparatide second line and denosumab third line. II That ranking is an unchanging rule for every fracture-risk group.
items.exp: These rankings are printed, but treatment selection depends on fracture risk, renal function and contraindications; very-high-risk patients may merit initial anabolic therapy. (Book p897)

items.q: A postmenopausal patient seeks therapy for severe hot flushes as well as bone loss. Which source-listed approach addresses the vasomotor indication but requires risk assessment?
opts: Raloxifene specifically to stop hot flushes
items.exp: The page links hormone replacement to severe hot flushes and lists breast-cancer, coronary and stroke risks; suitability depends on regimen and patient profile. (Book p897)

items.q: Which is the odd one out among adverse effects specifically listed for hormone replacement therapy here?
items.exp: The HRT entry names breast cancer, CHD and stroke; hypomagnesemic tetany is not in that adverse-effect list. (Book p897)

items.q: Assess strontium ranelate in this source: I It is described as purely antiresorptive with no bone-forming effect. II It is placed among first-choice routine therapies.
items.exp: Those are the two source statements. This historical treatment note should not be mistaken for an endorsement to prescribe it. (Book p897)

items.q: A patient requests calcitonin as the main long-term fracture-prevention drug. Which source assessment is most accurate?
opts: It is weakly antiresorptive and not recommended here
It is the strongest first-line hip-fracture preventive drug
It acts mainly by increasing RANKL signaling
It is the same anabolic pathway as teriparatide
items.exp: The page calls calcitonin weakly antiresorptive with minimal vertebral-fracture action and does not recommend it in this hierarchy. (Book p897)

items.q: Match the following raloxifene concepts — 1) Breast action 2) Bone action 3) Important adverse effect … A) Thromboembolism B) Estrogen antagonism C) Estrogen agonism
items.exp: Raloxifene is antiestrogenic in breast and estrogenic in bone; hot flushes and thromboembolism are listed adverse effects. The source's 'agonist everywhere' wording is too broad. (Book p897)

items.q: Evaluate: I Raloxifene can worsen hot flushes. II The source's vascular-antagonist shorthand means it protects against venous thromboembolism.
items.exp: The adverse-effect list explicitly includes hot flushes and thromboembolism; vascular shorthand must not reverse that risk. (Book p897)

items.q: Match the following named drug targets — 1) Odanacatib 2) Saracatinib 3) Romosozumab … A) Tyrosine kinase B) Cathepsin K C) Sclerostin
items.exp: The newer-drug list pairs these names with cathepsin K, tyrosine kinase and sclerostin inhibition respectively. (Book p897)

items.q: Assess the newer-drug list: I Odanacatib is paired with cathepsin K inhibition. II Every drug in the list is approved routine osteoporosis therapy.
items.exp: Odanacatib development was discontinued and saracatinib is not routine approved osteoporosis therapy; the source list must be read as pharmacology, not a prescribing formulary. (Book p897)
